passage:
"And that's why the vendor plan stays," said the director, moving straight to the next slide.
Shreya waited for a gap. There was none. Beside Shreya, Suraj whispered, "They never stop for breath."
"Four long stretches so far, and nobody under senior has spoken," Shreya whispered back. "Watch." Then, aloud, at the next comma: "Sir, may I take one minute on the vendor timing? It affects the March launch."
The director paused. "Go ahead."
Afterwards in the corridor Suraj said, "How did you dare?"
"I asked for a minute, not the floor," said Shreya. "My hands were shaking, though."

qa.q: What did Shreya ask the director at the next comma?
qa.a: For one minute on the vendor timing, because it affects the March launch.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling after asking, according to the corridor talk?
qa.a: Nervous. Shreya said the hands were shaking, even though the request sounded calm.

qa.q: What wording made the request easy for the director to grant?
qa.a: Asking for one minute, not the floor, and giving a reason tied to the March launch.

qa.q: How might the director see Shreya's request?
qa.a: As reasonable and useful, since the director paused and said "Go ahead"; the director may not have realised the juniors could find no gap.

grounding: A young employee sees juniors wait for gaps in a meeting and shows that asking the chair for a minute works.

passage: My name is Zainab. In my first quarter at a logistics company, the weekly review was mostly one person talking. Joseph, the senior manager, would speak in long stretches, and the juniors waited for gaps that never came. I watched it for three weeks. Divya tapped a pen. Others looked at the clock. Nobody was being rude; the room simply ran that way. So I practised. I wrote a sentence in my notebook, and at the end of a topic I said, "Joseph, could I add one point before we move on?" My voice cracked the first time. He said, "Of course," and listened. Since then I've treated it as a skill: name the gap, ask for a minute, keep it short.

qa.q: How long did Zainab watch the pattern in the weekly review before acting?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling the first time of asking for a point, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Nervous. The voice cracked the first time, even though the request was short and polite.

qa.q: What did Zainab do to prepare before speaking up in the review?
qa.a: Zainab wrote a sentence in a notebook and waited for the end of a topic to ask, "Joseph, could I add one point before we move on?"

qa.q: How might Joseph see the juniors' silence in the review?
qa.a: Joseph may not realise that the juniors are waiting for a gap; Joseph said "Of course" and listened once asked.

grounding: A young employee sees seniors talk in long stretches, learns to name a gap, and asks the chair for a minute.

passage:
Mentor's note, trainee programme, week 6.
In Monday's project meeting, Francis, one of our new trainees, noticed something I've been meaning to raise. The two senior managers spoke in long stretches for most of the hour. Reena, another trainee who'd done the customer survey, tried to come in three times. Each time a senior started speaking before she finished her first word.
Near the end, Francis caught the chair's eye and said, "Before we close, could Reena have two minutes? She ran the survey." The chair said, "Of course." Reena's two minutes changed the project timeline.
Afterwards Francis told me he'd been nervous but felt it was unfair. I've asked both trainees to lead a session on turn-taking for the next intake.

qa.q: How many times did Reena try to come in?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling before speaking up?
qa.a: Francis felt nervous but also troubled that it was unfair Reena kept getting cut off.

qa.q: Why did Francis's request to the chair work?
qa.a: It asked the chair for a specific short time for Reena and explained why, which respected the meeting's hierarchy while opening a gap.

qa.q: How might Reena have felt when she finally got her two minutes?
qa.a: She was probably relieved and valued, especially since her input changed the project timeline.

grounding: Shows a young employee noticing juniors waiting for gaps that never come and asking the chair for time, a learnable skill.

passage:
Wednesday.
Big review meeting today. Mr. Menon and Ms. Kaur talked for fifty of the sixty minutes. Pankaj and I, the two juniors, sat with our points ready. Every time there was a tiny pause, one of them filled it. Pankaj looked at me at one point and shrugged. He'd found a mistake in the cost sheet and never got to say it.
I felt small, then annoyed. Then I remembered what my old team lead used to do. When there were five minutes left, I raised my hand and said, "Sorry, can I add one thing before we close? Pankaj found an error in the cost sheet." Everyone turned. Mr. Menon said, "Go on, Pankaj."
Pankaj explained it in two minutes. Ms. Kaur actually thanked him. I'm going to ask for a juniors' slot on the agenda from now on.
Sonali

qa.q: How many of the sixty minutes did Mr. Menon and Ms. Kaur talk for?
qa.a: Fifty minutes.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling during the meeting?
qa.a: Sonali felt small and then annoyed, seeing juniors like Pankaj left without a chance to speak.

qa.q: What skill did Sonali use, and why did it work?
qa.a: Sonali named a gap by asking to add one thing before closing and pointing to Pankaj's finding, which gave him a clear turn.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt when Ms. Kaur thanked him?
qa.a: Pankaj probably felt relieved and valued after sitting silently with his point for most of the meeting.

grounding: Shows a young employee noticing seniors talking in long stretches while juniors wait, and learning to name a gap for a colleague.

passage: The monthly meeting at the block development office in Kalol ran the way it always did. The BDO spoke for twenty minutes, the senior engineer for fifteen, the accountant for ten more. Sudha, a year into her job as a junior assistant, watched Trisha beside her lean forward three times with her notebook open, then sit back each time as another senior voice filled the pause. Trisha had the only data on which village handpumps had failed. Sudha had seen this at every meeting. Nobody was rude; there just never was a gap. When the accountant finally paused, Sudha raised her hand and said to the BDO, "Sir, could Trisha have two minutes? She has the handpump data." The BDO blinked, then nodded. Trisha's voice shook on the first sentence, then steadied.

qa.q: How long did the senior engineer speak?
qa.a: The senior engineer spoke for fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling as she watched Trisha lean forward and sit back?
qa.a: Sudha felt frustrated for Trisha and a little anxious, knowing the gap Trisha was waiting for would never come.

qa.q: What made Sudha's request work?
qa.a: She asked the person chairing, named exactly how much time was needed and gave a reason, so it was easy for him to say yes.

qa.q: What was it like for Trisha to finally speak?
qa.a: She was nervous at first, her voice shaking, then steadied, probably relieved that her data was finally being heard.

grounding: Shows a young employee noticing that juniors never find a gap in a senior-led meeting and asking the chair for two minutes for a colleague.
